en: A road area where the speed limit is 30 miles per hour, common in built-up areas in the UK.
Anti-lock braking system that helps you steer while braking hard in an emergency.
Anti-lock braking system that helps you steer while braking hard in an emergency.
The pedal that increases engine power and vehicle speed (also called the gas pedal).
Cruise control that also adjusts speed to keep a gap from the vehicle ahead.
A recommended speed for safety that is not a legal maximum limit.
Automated external defibrillator: a device that can shock the heart back to rhythm.
The radio antenna on a vehicle, often a thin rod on the roof or rear.
Driving in a hostile or impatient way, such as tailgating or harsh speeding.
A braking system on many large vehicles that uses compressed air instead of only hydraulic fluid.
A safety cushion that inflates quickly in a crash to protect occupants.
The passage that lets air reach the lungs for breathing.
Being fully awake and ready to notice hazards and react quickly.
A different path to the same destination if the usual road is blocked.
A flashing amber warning light, often used on slow or working vehicles.
An orange warning light that flashes on a vehicle to make it more noticeable.
A rear-view mirror setting that reduces glare from headlights behind you at night.
ABS: brakes that help stop the wheels locking under hard braking.
Look far ahead and prepare early for what other vehicles will do.
A liquid mixed with water in the cooling system to stop it freezing in cold weather.
A recognised training course (often for safer driving) that insurers may treat as a discount factor.
A driving teacher officially approved to give paid lessons (ADI in the UK).
When tyres ride up on water and lose grip with the road surface.
A hand signal given by the driver to show other road users what you intend to do.
An approved place that can safely take hazardous items like car batteries.
A gearbox that changes gears for you, without a clutch pedal.
A stretch where cameras measure your average speed between two points.
An area where cameras check your average speed over a stretch of road.
The shafts that the wheels of a vehicle or trailer turn on.
A gate or arm that can block the road when a train is coming.
Areas around the vehicle that you cannot see in your mirrors alone.
A system that warns if a vehicle is in an area you cannot see in your mirrors.
A system that warns you about vehicles in areas you cannot see in the mirrors.
Fluid-filled swellings on the skin that can form after burns; do not burst them.
A UK disability parking badge that gives certain parking concessions.
A flashing blue warning light used by certain emergency or specialist vehicles.
Emergency warning lights used by police, fire, ambulance, and similar services.
The outer shell and panels of the vehicle (bonnet, wings, doors, etc.).
A short post on the road used to mark an island, edge, or obstruction.
The storage compartment at the back of a car (called the trunk in some countries).
A road junction painted with yellow criss-cross lines on the road surface.
Hydraulic fluid that transfers pressure from the brake pedal to the brakes.
Red lights at the rear that come on when you press the brake pedal.
Press the brake hard so the vehicle slows or stops suddenly.
When a vehicle stops working and can no longer be driven normally.
A service that helps if your vehicle stops working on the road.
A vehicle that helps remove or repair broken-down vehicles on the road.
Stops working so the vehicle cannot continue normally.
Dashed white road markings, often showing a boundary you may cross when safe.
A town or village area with buildings beside the road; street lighting often marks a 30 mph zone.
Towns or villages with buildings close to the road; a 30 mph limit often applies with street lights.
The protective bar at the front or rear of a vehicle designed to absorb minor impacts.
When vehicles pack closely together, often causing sudden braking waves.
A lane reserved for buses (and sometimes taxis/cycles) during the times shown on signs.
A lane reserved mainly for buses (and sometimes taxis or cycles) at certain times.
Lanes reserved mainly for buses (and sometimes taxis or cycles).
A trailer designed for living or camping, towed behind a vehicle.
The part of the road used by vehicles, not the pavement or verge.
People injured in an accident or emergency.
An injured person in an accident.
The strip or barrier that separates the two directions of traffic on a dual carriageway.
The unique identification number stamped on the vehicle's frame.
Repeated firm pushes on the centre of the chest during CPR to pump blood.
A child seat or similar device that holds a child safely in the vehicle.
A special seat that holds a child safely with the correct restraints.
A road marked so that stopping on the main carriageway is tightly restricted.
The pedal that disconnects the engine from the wheels so you can change gear.
The pedal/system that disconnects the engine from the wheels when changing gear.
To roll without engine drive (e.g. in neutral), which reduces control.
Rolling without a gear engaged, so the engine does not help slow the vehicle.
Rolling along with the clutch pressed or in neutral, so the engine is not driving the wheels.
Rolling down a slope without using the engine to help control speed.
A steering column designed to fold in a crash to reduce injury.
A crash when vehicles or objects hit each other.
A wide motor insurance level that can cover your own vehicle as well as damage to others.
Heavy, slow-moving traffic when roads are overcrowded.
Fees charged to drive into certain busy city zones to reduce traffic.
Say or show the opposite of something else.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
An area where parking is controlled by signs and marked bays at set times.
The liquid in the engine cooling system that helps stop the engine overheating.
Support legs at the corners of a caravan used to keep it stable when parked, not while towing.
Posts with decreasing bars (3, 2, 1) showing how close you are to a motorway exit.
A narrow rural road, often with limited space and visibility.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions (and breaths) to help someone not breathing.
An extra uphill lane for slow vehicles so faster traffic is not held up.
A junction where two roads cross, usually forming a plus-sign shape.
A junction where two roads cross each other.
A system that holds a set speed without keeping your foot on the accelerator.
Moves suddenly into your lane or gap with little space in front of you.
A part of the road marked for cyclists, shown by a bicycle symbol and lane lines.
A part of the road reserved for cyclists, often marked with a bicycle symbol.
A path or lane intended for bicycles.
A person riding a bicycle on the road.
Hazardous materials (chemicals, fuels, etc.) needing special transport rules.
A light on the instrument panel that alerts you to a vehicle fault or important status.
Temporarily blind someone with bright light.
Temporarily blinded or unable to see clearly because of bright lights.
Temporarily blinds other drivers with bright light so they cannot see clearly.
Blinding other drivers with bright lights, such as brake lights in a queue at night.
Blinding other drivers with bright lights so they cannot see properly.
Scattered pieces of wreckage, objects, or rubbish left after a crash.
A careful driving style that anticipates hazards and leaves a safety margin.
A portable device that can deliver an electric shock to try to restart a heart in cardiac arrest.
A control that clears mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
Controls that clear mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
White diamond road markings that show a lane reserved for particular vehicles.
The cover that seals the diesel filler opening; if loose, fuel can spill onto the road.
Switch from full beam to dipped (lower) beam so oncoming or overtaking drivers are not dazzled.
Headlights aimed lower so they light the road without dazzling oncoming drivers.
Headlights aimed lower so they light the road without dazzling oncoming drivers.
Low points in the road that can hide traffic until you are close.
Parking spaces reserved for vehicles displaying a valid Blue Badge.
Getting off a bicycle (or motorcycle) to walk beside it.
Temporary signs that send traffic along a different route around a closure or roadworks.
The side mirrors mounted on the doors, used to see traffic beside and behind you.
A warning that two bends follow closely, one after the other.
Parked beside another parked vehicle, blocking a lane or space.
Two white lines along the centre of the road that restrict crossing and parking.
Two yellow lines at the kerb meaning no waiting at any time (unless signs say otherwise).
Metal lids over drains in the road surface; they can be slippery when wet.
Gradually moving sideways so the vehicle leaves its traffic lane.
Driving after drinking alcohol or taking drugs that impair your ability to drive.
A driver-assistance feature that detects tired driving and alerts you.
Technology that helps the driver with safety, control, or alerts.
A private path from a house or property that joins the public road.
Official papers such as your licence and insurance that prove you can drive legally.
The official card that shows you are allowed to drive certain vehicles.
Sleepiness that slows your thinking and reactions while driving.
Feeling sleepy or half-asleep, so your reactions and attention are reduced.
A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
Extra pedals for the supervisor or instructor to help control the car.
The period of fading light after sunset when visibility drops.
Move the car forward very slowly, a little at a time, to improve your view before joining the road.
Move the vehicle slowly ahead a short distance.
Stuck inside the wound (for example glass or metal); do not pull it out yourself.
Come out onto the road from a side road, driveway, or similar entrance.
A marked bay beside a motorway for stopping in an emergency when there is no hard shoulder.
